what: An AI gateway is one API that sits in front of many model providers. It picks a model for each call, retries or falls back when one fails, and applies keys, budgets, caching, logging and guardrails in one place.
like: Like a travel agent: you say where you want to go, and they pick the airline, rebook you if a flight is cancelled, and keep every receipt.
why: Switch or mix providers without changing app code
Fallbacks keep the product up when one provider rate-limits or goes down
One place for keys, budgets, caching, logs and safety checks

nodes.t: Keys and limits|per-key RPM, TPM, budget

steps.d: Apps call one OpenAI-style endpoint with a virtual key. The gateway translates to each provider's format, so swapping models is a config change, not a code change.
Each key carries requests per minute (RPM), tokens per minute (TPM) and a spend budget. Over the limit, the caller gets a clear 429 instead of a surprise bill.
An identical (or, with semantic caching, a very similar) prompt can be answered from cache, skipping the model call entirely.
Guardrails screen the prompt. The router then picks a model by cost, latency, quality or a rule, for example a small model first for easy queries.
On a 429 or 5xx it retries, then moves to the next model or provider in the list. In a cascade, a weak or low-confidence answer escalates to the big model.
Every call records model, tokens, cost, latency and errors per key and team, which feeds dashboards, budgets and debugging.

choices.d: Self-host LiteLLM proxy or Kong for control and data residency; use OpenRouter or Cloudflare AI Gateway as a managed service; Azure API Management fits teams already on Azure.
Fixed per feature, weighted split for A/B tests, lowest latency, lowest cost, or semantic (match the prompt to a model). Start simple and measure.
Order models and providers by preference. Decide which errors trigger it: rate limits and 5xx yes, bad requests no. Separate fallbacks for context-too-long and content-policy errors.
A few retries with backoff, then take a failing deployment out of rotation for a cooldown window so you stop hammering it.
Small model first, escalate when a check (confidence score, validator, judge) says the answer is weak. Tune the threshold on an eval set to trade cost for quality.

instead.why: General API gateway without token-aware limits or model fallbacks
Retry and fallback logic inside one service only
Just the caching part, without routing or keys
Call one provider directly when you only use one model

breaks.d: The backup model formats answers differently or is weaker.
breaks.see: Parse errors or quality drop during a provider incident
breaks.fix: Run evals on every model in the fallback list and pin output schemas

breaks.d: Every client retries a rate-limited provider at once.
breaks.see: 429s rise and latency climbs across all teams
breaks.fix: Backoff with jitter, honour Retry-After, cooldown failing deployments

breaks.d: All AI traffic flows through one service.
breaks.see: Every AI feature slows when the gateway does
breaks.fix: Run several replicas behind a load balancer and keep it stateless

breaks.d: The backup model is far pricier than the primary.
breaks.fix: Budget-aware routing and price-checked fallback lists

breaks.d: Spend tracking needs its database; if that is down, limits are skipped.
breaks.fix: Monitor the spend store and alert when it is unreachable

say: All model calls go through an AI gateway like LiteLLM proxy, so apps use one API and we can change providers in config.
Each team gets a virtual key with RPM, TPM and a monthly budget, and every call is logged with tokens and cost.
On a 429 or 5xx we retry with backoff, then fall back to a second provider, and a failing deployment cools down for a while.
For cost we cascade: a small model answers first and we escalate to the big model only when a check says the answer is weak.

followups.q: Why not call providers directly from each service?
followups.a: Every team would re-build keys, retries, fallbacks, logging and budgets, each a bit differently. A gateway does it once and gives one spend view across the company.

followups.q: How do you choose which model handles a request?
followups.a: Start with a fixed model per feature. Then add rules by task type or prompt length, latency-based routing, or a cascade. Judge every rule by cost per good answer on an eval set.

followups.q: What errors should trigger a fallback?
followups.a: Rate limits (429), server errors (5xx), timeouts, and context-too-long or content-policy errors to a model that can handle them. Plain bad requests should fail fast, not fall back.
A little for the extra network hop, kept small by running it close to your apps. Cache hits and smarter routing usually save far more than that.

today: By 2026 AI gateways are a standard platform piece: LiteLLM, OpenRouter, Cloudflare AI Gateway, Azure API Management and Kong all offer routing, fallbacks, token limits, caching and spend tracking.

check.q: Your main provider returns 429 for a minute. What should the gateway do?
check.a: Retry with backoff, then fall back to the next model
d: Return the error to every user
check.why: Rate limits are short; backoff plus a fallback list keeps the product up.

check.a: Try a small model first, escalate weak answers to a bigger one
d: Sending long prompts to the cheapest model
check.why: Most queries are easy, so the cheap model handles them and cost drops.

check.q: Which limit protects you from one team running up a huge bill?
check.a: A spend budget on that team's virtual key
check.why: Budgets cap money per key or team; RPM and TPM cap speed.

check.q: A fallback model starts returning broken JSON during an outage. Best fix?
check.a: Eval every fallback model and enforce the output schema
check.why: Fallbacks only help if the backup model meets the same contract.
